title: Steady-stream Capacity and Queueing Heuristics
content:
Purpose
Quick working note: capture an alternative framing for sizing continuous/stream batching where traffic is steady (non-bursty) and tenant-level budgets are enforced. This is a lightweight model intended to be translated into a small spreadsheet and a follow-up A/B experiment. Unlike prior docs that focus on arrival burst decomposition and window-based batching, this sketch centers on smoothing token pressure, allocating concurrency per-tenant, and making soft-queueing thresholds explicit in cost accounting.

High-level goals
- Provide a simple spreadsheet that product/platform can use to pick: reserved concurrency per-tenant, target batch window (ms), and expected p95 under steady arrivals.
- Make unit cost sensitivity explicit to token mix (prompt vs. completion length) and stream vs. single-turn workloads.
- Produce a small set of operational knobs for Dedicated: per-tenant concurrency budget, soft-queueing threshold, and dynamic backpressure multiplier.

Assumptions (steady-stream regime)
- Arrival process: approximately Poisson-like but low variance; coefficient of variation (CV) of inter-arrival ~0.8.
- Typical request token distribution: prompt = 40 tokens (median), completion = 80 tokens (median) — parameterize in sheet.
- Serving instance: A100-80GB equivalent; baseline tokens/sec at single-threaded decode (non-quantized) = 1600 tokens/s for the model under test.
- Batch assembly cost: small per-batch overhead (O) = 3 ms per batch; per-token decoding cost scales linearly.
- Concurrency slots are GPU-backed workers; each slot accepts one active request but can host batching across requests.

Key variables to expose in the spreadsheet
- N_slots (concurrency budget) per tenant (integer)
- target_batch_ms (batching window) — how long we wait to collect tokens before running forward pass
- avg_tokens_per_request (param)
- tokens_per_sec_per_slot (computed) = tokens/s decode * utilization_factor (depends on batching)
- batch_overhead_ms (O)
- expected_batch_size = arrival_rate_per_slot * target_batch_ms
- p95_latency_estimate = queueing_time + service_time + batch_overhead_penalty (see formulas below)
- cost_per_token_usd = gpu_hourly_cost / (tokens_per_hour_effective)

Formulas (spreadsheet-ready, use guard rails in cells)
1) arrival_rate_per_tenant = tenant_RPS * avg_tokens_per_request (tokens/s)
2) arrival_rate_per_slot = arrival_rate_per_tenant / N_slots (tokens/s per slot)
3) expected_batch_tokens = arrival_rate_per_slot * target_batch_ms/1000
4) effective_tokens_per_second_per_slot = decode_tokens_per_second * batch_efficiency_factor
   - batch_efficiency_factor = 1 - (batch_overhead_ms / (batch_overhead_ms + per_batch_processing_ms))
   - per_batch_processing_ms = expected_batch_tokens / decode_tokens_per_second * 1000
5) service_time_ms_for_request = (avg_tokens_per_request / expected_batch_tokens) * per_batch_processing_ms + batch_overhead_ms
6) queueing_expected_ms = (target_batch_ms / 2) * (when using fixed window) OR use M/M/1 approximation for soft queue: 1/(mu - lambda)
7) p95_estimate_ms = queueing_p95 + service_time_ms_for_request + small_network_tail (10 ms)

Sample sheet numbers (toy baseline)
- tenant_RPS = 0.75 req/s
- avg_tokens_per_request = 120 tokens
- N_slots = 4
- target_batch_ms = 40 ms
- decode_tokens_per_second = 1600 tokens/s
- batch_overhead_ms = 3 ms
Compute:
- arrival_rate_per_tenant = 0.75 * 120 = 90 tokens/s
- arrival_rate_per_slot = 90 / 4 = 22.5 tokens/s
- expected_batch_tokens = 22.5 * 0.04 = 0.9 tokens (indicates we often get <1 token per window; i.e., window too small for this RPS)
- per_batch_processing_ms = 0.9 / 1600 * 1000 = 0.56 ms
- batch_efficiency_factor = 1 - (3 / (3 + 0.56)) = ~0.157 => very inefficient; effective_tokens_per_second_per_slot ~ 250 tokens/s * 0.157 = ~250*0.157 (adjust decode number to 1600 -> effective 251) approx 40 tokens/s
- Observations: with low RPS and small window, batch overhead dominates => increase target_batch_ms or reduce N_slots.

Policies and heuristics (operational)
1) Min-batch guard: if expected_batch_tokens < 8, increase window to hit target = 8 tokens (configurable). Rationale: below ~8 tokens, overhead amortization is poor for A100-like instances.
2) Concurrency floor per-tenant: set minimum N_slots = max(1, ceil(tenant_peak_rps * min_concurrency_factor)) where min_concurrency_factor defaults to 2 for multi-turn workloads.
3) Soft-queueing threshold: allow queue depth up to Q_soft = N_slots * 3 before rejecting; use backpressure multiplier to pace upstream clients when queue > Q_soft.
4) Cost-aware slot reclaim: if tenant sustained utilization < 25% for 15m, autoshrink N_slots by 1 (but keep above floor). Avoid oscillation with 5m cooldown.
5) Tail-latency guardrail: keep a path for single-slot low-latency work (fast-path) where small responses (<32 tokens) are routed to specialized low-batch pipelines when p95 breach is predicted.

Sensitivity checks to add to spreadsheet
- Vary avg_tokens_per_request across [32, 120, 400] and show cost_per_1000_prompts impact.
- Sweep target_batch_ms in [10, 40, 120, 250] ms and plot p95 vs token-unit-cost.
- Sweep N_slots from 1..16 for a tenant to find diminishing returns on throughput and p95 improvement.

Experiment plan (small, quick)
A) Bandit test across three buckets for low-volume tenants (<1 req/s):
   - Arm 1: window = 40ms, N_slots = 2 (baseline)
   - Arm 2: adaptive window -> min(500ms, 8 tokens / arrival_rate_per_slot * 1000)
   - Arm 3: N_slots auto-shrink to 1 + burst buffer
Measure: p50/p95/90 token cost, aborts, queue length percentiles, client error rate. Run 48 hours per bucket.

B) Throughput-stress: synthetic traffic ramp to 3x expected RPS; verify that soft-queueing and reclaim heuristics keep p95 under SLA for 99% of tenants and redirect others to fallback model.

Metrics to collect (per-tenant and global)
- realized_batch_size distribution (tokens and request count)
- batch_wait_time_ms histogram
- service_time_ms histogram
- slot_utilization (percent of decode time occupied)
- cost_per_token_usd approximation (compute + infra amortized)
- p50/p90/p95 latencies; correlate with batch size and queue length

Risk/unknowns
- Some models show non-linear scaling with batch size due to attention kernel behavior; above formulas assume linear token decoding time which may under/overestimate at large batches. Add kernel-level correction factor in sheet when model-specific perf numbers available.
- Multi-tenant interference on shared GPUs: our model assumes per-slot isolation; if packing or multiplexing happens, queueing behavior changes. Note to adjust when using shared-pool mode.

Action items and next steps
- [Maya] build simple Google Sheet with the above parameters + prefilled sample scenarios (due 2024-07-17).
- [Ravi] instrument tenant-level batch-size, wait-time, and slot-utilization metrics in prometheus (add labels: tenant_id, slot_id) (due 2024-07-24).
- [Anna] create the A/B experiment JIRA (JIRA-9984) and produce experiment spec for traffic buckets (due 2024-07-21).
- [Liam] get kernel perf numbers for the two most common model families and provide correction factors (due 2024-07-30).

Notes to reviewer
- This is intentionally pragmatic and spreadsheet-focused. The aim is to get a conservative but deployable set of defaults for low-throughput tenants that suffer from batch-overhead waste. The follow-ups should produce a small library function that recommends (N_slots, target_batch_ms, min_tokens_per_batch) per-tenant at signup.

References and context links

End of doc.
